Ebola paediatrician

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A first hand account of a South African Paediatrician who is about to go back to treat Ebola patients

Summary:
The self sacrifice of a doctor on the front line treating children with Ebola. What does it take mentally, physically and emotionally.

Further information:
Dr Juli Switala thought about contracting Ebola every single day. She had to. Her quest to help heal ill children in Sierra Leone had suddenly turned into a no-touch mission.
“The way you live in a society that is affected by Ebola is completely different to everything you do at home,” said the paediatrician from Doctors Without Borders (MSF).
“You sign a contract to say you won’t touch anybody. You don’t hug anyone. You wear gloves all the time. You can’t not think about contracting Ebola.
“You use chlorine in the water you drink, you wash your clothes with chlorine.
“If you’re cooking potatoes, you have to wash them with chlorine because someone with Ebola could have touched them before you. Ebola becomes a way of life.”
Switala returned to South Africa two weeks ago after spending several months in Sierra Leone, where she was part of the paediatric team at MSF’s Gondama referral centre, a 220-bed hospital offering emergency paediatric and obstetric services.
But then, in June, Ebola hit the region. Ultimately, she would run a 20-bed isolation unit while a new treatment centre was set up, and as the outbreak worsened, she became the paediatric Ebola referent for the hospital.
Now that she is back home, she thought her friends and family would be scared to touch her.
“I expected people to be wary of touching me but they are putting out their hands for me to shake.
“With a lot of my colleagues, people are nervous to touch them, or they aren’t comfortable if they are around their kids. I’m so glad that hasn’t happened to me. I’m confident I’m not sick, and if I was I would know what to do.”
In Sierra Leone, it’s peak season for diseases like malaria and cholera that affect children.
It should be the busiest time at the Gondama referral hospital, but instead, because of fears of contracting Ebola, it has become a ghost town, she said.
“The hospital has a capacity of 200 beds. When I left there were 50 patients. People are too scared to come to hospital. And watching that is terrible. You know it’s not that the kids are not sick, but they are dying out there from diseases other than Ebola.
“Their families are too scared to bring them into hospital. It’s heartbreaking to go to work every day and there’s three fewer patients admitted than the day before.”
The hospital’s obstetrics division had to shut because of the risk. Indeed, so many clinics have closed in the region, it is “apocalyptic”.
Expectant mothers are unable to have caesareans, and TB and HIV patients are defaulting on treatment.
Switala was surprised by how many children have Ebola: once she started to work in the isolation unit she found that a quarter of the admissions were under 18.
“It’s not a terminal disease. There is a high fatality rate but our aim is to optimise treatment to patients who can be cured.
“When people are discharged, everyone claps for them, it’s wonderful. Tomorrow might be their turn.
“Many patients, I can see, will not make it, and then I talk to them, rub their backs, which is worth more than 1 000 blood tests and a million drugs.
“It’s about keeping them comfortable and giving them a dignified death, knowing you protected their family or others who could have contracted the disease from them.”
Solving the epidemic, she said, is “about trusting people to come forward”.
“Some patients know they are at risk and immediately isolate themselves. Then there are others who try to hide the symptoms, because they are scared.”
The world needs to step up to counter the worsening pandemic.
“There are many deaths from diseases other than Ebola that are because of Ebola, like people dying from car accidents or in childbirth because they have nowhere to go.”
Other countries should not feel immune, she warned. “West Africa is being left to burn because everyone thinks it won’t affect them, but it will.”
Switala will head back to the hospital at the end of the week. “I have no romantic ideas about Ebola. But I was there when it started with the staff and I want to see it through.”

Press Release:


Ebola Doctors
The war on Ebola is far from won. International promises of assistance have been woefully inadequate. What is it like for the doctors treating a disease that has caused hysteria across the USA and wreaked havoc in Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea? Carte Blanche finds out from two dedicated South African doctors working with Medicines Sans Frontiers.


Script:


EBOLA OCTOBER FINAL SCRIPT

Commentary One
On Monday this week Cape Town paediatrician, Dr Juli Switala flew back to Sierra Leone for another month on the frontlines of Ebola, with Medicines Sans Frontiers

Juli
I feel the safest time of my day is in the isolation unit – I am wearing protective clothing, there are other people watching me if I make a mistake – what is difficult is going home and making sure you don’t touch your mouth or use someone else’ s cup. If you had to watch some one falling you wouldn’t be able to help them up

Commentary Two
For a second time Julie flew back to a no touching zone, elbow handshakes and the smell of chlorine hanging heavy in the air

Juli
You start to feel it after a few days that your hair is really dry, your skin gets horrible, coffee doesn’t taste right. When you get to the hospital there is more chlorine.. washing your hands, every time you get into a vehicle.. washing your hands. Chlorine is just a part of your life

Commentary Three
And there are strict rules around food preparation

Juli
All our fruit and veg needs to be rinsed in quite a high concentration of chlorine before we cook it, any bread that you buy could have been touched by somebody so you re- bake all of your bread

Commentary Four
Julie first went to Sierra Leone in June arriving just days ahead of the outbreak there. She travelled roads like these to Bo Town. At first Ebola was just a rumour.

Juli
I just happened to be on duty the night that first patient died and filling in that death certificate and writing Ebola – this is just something I never thought I would have to do

Commentary five
As a few cases mushroomed quickly to an epidemic, she says she felt like a waiter on the titanic

Juli
And all that you are trying to do in the beginning is serve the soup hot. Hearing that there were problems outside but thinking it wont affect us – but eventually the water starts seeping in and at some point it is knee deep. Then you have to throw out your soup and use the bowels to throw out the water and I feel that Ebola is like the iceberg, where once the Titanic has hit there, its not the iceberg that is really causing the problem, it’s the water.

Commentary Six
For Julie, the water symbolizes diseases other than Ebola that are now killing people, who are terrified of the hospitals. It’s a double humanitarian crisis she told a group of journalists in Johannesburg before she left

JULI
I have done things I never thought I would - have sat pushing blood into a child through a syringe because I knew he didn’t have the hour it would take for the blood to run freely through a drip. He survived but you really feel like you are doing Macgyver medicine!

Commentary Seven
Sometimes the doctors had no choice but to stand back and watch people die rather than put their team’s safety at risk- Caesarians and resuscitation became too dangerous for them to perform.

Julie press conference
As a team we had to make the decision that we were no longer going to resus any children besides neo-nates because the risk of body fluid exposure and the possible benefits just didn’t weigh up, and that was very, very, hard.

Commentary eight
Epidemiologist Andrew Medina-Marino first spoke to Carte Blanche from Liberia in August. He has kept a record of the case numbers there -231 when he arrived, to nearly 4000 in early October.

Andrew
What happened from when I got there to when I left there was a tripling of the number of cases in Liberia


Commentary nine
He too, emphasizes the high death toll from other diseases that people shouldn’t be dying from.

Andrew
Up to now there are 200 health care workers that have become infected in Liberia of which slightly over a 100 have died and so when you think about the few docs and nurses that were in the country and killing off 100 of them… and so it’s a health system that is in collapse, or has collapsed.

Commentary ten
4900. That’s around the number of Ebola deaths recorded so far. The Centre for Disease control predicts the possibility of 5000 to 10 000 new cases a week till December.

Devi Link
It feels almost apocalyptic – a galloping epidemic, a small band of doctors on the frontlines and an international response that came far to late

Commentary eleven
Medicines Sans Frontiers started ringing alarm bells in June.

Andrew
And I think it wasn’t until only August that W.H.O declared the situation an emergency and so we lost that entire time, um I would like to think that in the next month or two that all the appropriate resources will be put on ground, but again in another month or two you are going to get another few thousand cases

Commentary twelve
In August The W.H.O promised 100 million dollars. But at the world’s largest Ebola treatment center in Liberia where Jens Pederson was based, it never came.

Jens Pederson Humanitarian Affairs Advisor MSF
We are constantly finding our selves if not one, but two steps behind in our efforts to stop the transmission of Ebola. We have heard many, many big promises four or five weeks ago from various states, various international bodies and I can assure you a lot of it remains promises that are not translated into action on the ground


Commentary thirteen
Ebola is now affecting these economies as GDP declines, food security is threatened, shops close, and orphans are shunned by fearful societies.

Sharon Ekambaram Head of MSF SA DNA unit
And MSF is really angry that the world and the international community is failing the people of Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

Andrew
I think the W.H. O could have done better job. I would like to think that they are stepping up now, but I think that the fruits of that labour have yet to materialize

Commentary fourteen
Meanwhile American hysteria over a handful of cases has angered many Africans, and baffled doctors like Stefan Kruger who worked at the epicenter in Sierra Leone, where he could see 15- 20 new cases per day.

Stefan
A lot of the time you switch on to international media and the focus is immediately how wealthy countries are protecting themselves from Ebola but that is not what Ebola is about – Ebola is not about Europe and North America – Ebola is about West Africa and its wreaking havoc there!

Commentary fifteen
Stefan is now back in Sierra Leone, working ten- hour days, nine days at a time for about 6 weeks. Sometimes he feels their attempts are feeble.

Stefan
A lot of the time you try as hard as you possibly can and the patient still die
I think it is only natural to reach a point where you say is any of what we are doing, actually making a difference to the overall survival rate, but even though we will never know how significant it is, we are compelled to keep trying

Commentary sixteen
On his day off he volunteers to take the 37% who survive back to their villagers.

Up sound clapping …

Commentary seventeen
Survivors get a new set of clothes … each life saved - a celebration. Stefan never thought this grandmother whose family died, would make it.

Stefan
But she kept on getting better and she looked after the young children that had been orphaned and we were actually tempted to keep her in for a few days, because she was such a big help… and it was my last day of mission.. so I got to take her back to her village and that was quite a special experience as well

Up sound music

Commentary eighteen
Young Mahmadee Sayon also defied the statistics

Harrison Sakela was Liberia’s first survivor. He now works as a guard at MSF – immune to the disease surrounding him.

Julie
You open one last gate and say go…
Devi
You are free
Juli
You are free! And they are the only people that you can hug because they are no risk to you -and that is amazing those are some of the best hugs I have had in my life!
Devi
How has this experience changed you?
Julie
I think the most important thing is you become aware of your own mortality and that you want to live your life in a way where you are not scared of dying and you also become very appreciative of very small things – every day that you have to spend with your friends your family become very valuable
Devi
But then what is it like sitting on the other end of the world doing this?
Juli
I have to
Why?
Juli
I can’t explain it. If you are called to do something you have to do it
…I am at peace with where I am what I have done what I have seen. I struggled to leave until they could guarantee I could come back

Commentary nineteen
If there is a light, it comes from Nigeria and Senegal, declared Ebola free this week. But on Friday a New York doctor was positively diagnosed and the disease has spread to Mali. It looks like Ebola may be with us for a while.

Andrew
Best-case scenario end of 2015 but if you look at the track record of the international response I cant imagine this not ending before 2016.

Commentary twenty
The Centre for Disease control’s worst- case scenario figures are staggering. 1.4 million cases by the 20th January

Andrew
The world should be scared to high heaven – if it gets to 1.4 million all bets are off I don’t know what is going to happen

THE END

PROMO ONE 15 seconds
South African doctors spurn the comforts of a private practice to help fight the deadly Ebola epidemic
Julie
I think the most important thing is you become aware of your own mortality and that you want to live your life in a way where you are not scared of dying

PROMO TWO
Ebola is out of control and no one knows when it will end
Andrew
Best-case scenario end of 2015 but if you look at the track record of the international response I cant imagine this ending into 2016.

Stefan A lot of the time you try as hard as you possibly can and the patient still die I think it is only natural to reach a point where you say is any of what we are doing, actually making a difference to the overall survival rate, but even though we will never know how significant it is, we are compelled to keep trying Commentary sixteen On his day off he volunteers to take the 37% who survive back to their villagers. Up sound clapping … Commentary seventeen Survivors get a new set of clothes … each life saved - a celebration. Stefan never thought this grandmother whose family died, would make it. Stefan But she kept on getting better and she looked after the young children that had been orphaned and we were actually tempted to keep her in for a few days, because she was such a big help… and it was my last day of mission.. so I got to take her back to her village and that was quite a special experience as well Up sound music Commentary eighteen Young Mahmadee Sayon also defied the statistics Harrison Sakela was Liberia’s first survivor. He now works as a guard at MSF – immune to the disease surrounding him. Julie You open one last gate and say go… Devi You are free Juli You are free! And they are the only people that you can hug because they are no risk to you -and that is amazing those are some of the best hugs I have had in my life! Devi How has this experience changed you? Julie I think the most important thing is you become aware of your own mortality and that you want to live your life in a way where you are not scared of dying and you also become very appreciative of very small things – every day that you have to spend with your friends your family become very valuable Devi But then what is it like sitting on the other end of the world doing this? Juli I have to Why? Juli I can’t explain it. If you are called to do something you have to do it …I am at peace with where I am what I have done what I have seen. I struggled to leave until they could guarantee I could come back Commentary nineteen If there is a light, it comes from Nigeria and Senegal, declared Ebola free this week. But on Friday a New York doctor was positively diagnosed and the disease has spread to Mali. It looks like Ebola may be with us for a while. Andrew Best-case scenario end of 2015 but if you look at the track record of the international response I cant imagine this not ending before 2016. Commentary twenty The Centre for Disease control’s worst- case scenario figures are staggering. 1.4 million cases by the 20th January Andrew The world should be scared to high heaven – if it gets to 1.4 million all bets are off I don’t know what is going to happen THE END PROMO ONE 15 seconds South African doctors spurn the comforts of a private practice to help fight the deadly Ebola epidemic Julie I think the most important thing is you become aware of your own mortality and that you want to live your life in a way where you are not scared of dying PROMO TWO Ebola is out of control and no one knows when it will end Andrew Best-case scenario end of 2015 but if you look at the track record of the international response I cant imagine this ending into 2016. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A first hand account of a South African Paediatrician who is about to go back to treat Ebola patients
metadata.Summary: The self sacrifice of a doctor on the front line treating children with Ebola. What does it take mentally, physically and emotionally.
metadata.Further information: Dr Juli Switala thought about contracting Ebola every single day. She had to. Her quest to help heal ill children in Sierra Leone had suddenly turned into a no-touch mission. “The way you live in a society that is affected by Ebola is completely different to everything you do at home,” said the paediatrician from Doctors Without Borders (MSF). “You sign a contract to say you won’t touch anybody. You don’t hug anyone. You wear gloves all the time. You can’t not think about contracting Ebola. “You use chlorine in the water you drink, you wash your clothes with chlorine. “If you’re cooking potatoes, you have to wash them with chlorine because someone with Ebola could have touched them before you. Ebola becomes a way of life.” Switala returned to South Africa two weeks ago after spending several months in Sierra Leone, where she was part of the paediatric team at MSF’s Gondama referral centre, a 220-bed hospital offering emergency paediatric and obstetric services. But then, in June, Ebola hit the region. Ultimately, she would run a 20-bed isolation unit while a new treatment centre was set up, and as the outbreak worsened, she became the paediatric Ebola referent for the hospital. Now that she is back home, she thought her friends and family would be scared to touch her. “I expected people to be wary of touching me but they are putting out their hands for me to shake. “With a lot of my colleagues, people are nervous to touch them, or they aren’t comfortable if they are around their kids. I’m so glad that hasn’t happened to me. I’m confident I’m not sick, and if I was I would know what to do.” In Sierra Leone, it’s peak season for diseases like malaria and cholera that affect children. It should be the busiest time at the Gondama referral hospital, but instead, because of fears of contracting Ebola, it has become a ghost town, she said. “The hospital has a capacity of 200 beds. When I left there were 50 patients. People are too scared to come to hospital. And watching that is terrible. You know it’s not that the kids are not sick, but they are dying out there from diseases other than Ebola. “Their families are too scared to bring them into hospital. It’s heartbreaking to go to work every day and there’s three fewer patients admitted than the day before.” The hospital’s obstetrics division had to shut because of the risk. Indeed, so many clinics have closed in the region, it is “apocalyptic”. Expectant mothers are unable to have caesareans, and TB and HIV patients are defaulting on treatment. Switala was surprised by how many children have Ebola: once she started to work in the isolation unit she found that a quarter of the admissions were under 18. “It’s not a terminal disease. There is a high fatality rate but our aim is to optimise treatment to patients who can be cured. “When people are discharged, everyone claps for them, it’s wonderful. Tomorrow might be their turn. “Many patients, I can see, will not make it, and then I talk to them, rub their backs, which is worth more than 1 000 blood tests and a million drugs. “It’s about keeping them comfortable and giving them a dignified death, knowing you protected their family or others who could have contracted the disease from them.” Solving the epidemic, she said, is “about trusting people to come forward”. “Some patients know they are at risk and immediately isolate themselves. Then there are others who try to hide the symptoms, because they are scared.” The world needs to step up to counter the worsening pandemic. “There are many deaths from diseases other than Ebola that are because of Ebola, like people dying from car accidents or in childbirth because they have nowhere to go.” Other countries should not feel immune, she warned. “West Africa is being left to burn because everyone thinks it won’t affect them, but it will.” Switala will head back to the hospital at the end of the week. “I have no romantic ideas about Ebola. But I was there when it started with the staff and I want to see it through.”
